log.entry: Commission accepted: Leaf & Wilder — plant store in Riverton

Leaf & Wilder: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a plant store the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
Leaf & Wilder: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

Leaf & Wilder: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D1, never just shrink..

Leaf & Wilder: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. D2 gets its own arrangement from the book — the plant store reads differently here..

Leaf & Wilder: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. D3 gets its own arrangement from the book — the plant store reads differently here..

Leaf & Wilder: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D4, never just shrink..

Leaf & Wilder: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D5, never just shrink..

Leaf & Wilder: Reason about colour — what works where — Global colour law locked: hero washes, card tints and CTA styles are chosen per page from RECIPE_POOL — every recipe must clear its WCAG target before it is allowed. The palette (Fern Garden, triadic) provides the roles; dark-mode tokens re-derive and re-check.

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a plant store sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a plant store

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a plant store site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the plant store spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the plant store's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a plant store visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

brief.audience: plant store regulars who notice details
brief.promise: Living things, sold kindly. Leaf & Wilder keeps that promise in Riverton.
brief.cityStory: Every plant is quarantined and pest-checked before it hits the floor — and we do it in Riverton.

D1.why: Pocket Bento — A 2×1 headline cell opens, then 1×1 cells stack at the locked 12px gap and 20px radius. (source: Setproduct bento collapsed to one column)

D2.why: Zen Padding — Section padding ×1.25, gutters 24px; fewer, larger blocks per screen. (source: Material comfortable spacing scale on tablets)

D3.why: Directory — Tinted list bands with dense two-column link lists — built for scanning, not reading. (source: Directory/index pattern (layer-cake scanning))

D4.why: Wide Spread — 8-col story with 4-col side field; the mega footer with newsletter closes. (source: Magazine fields + mega footer (v2 Folio at desktop))

D5.why: Ultra Grid — Centered hero over a strict 5-col feature grid; identical cards. (source: 5-column feature grid (v2 D5 law))

log.entry: Commission accepted: Mat & Quiet — yoga atelier in Calder

Mat & Quiet: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a yoga atelier the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
Mat & Quiet: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

Mat & Quiet: Compose visitor persona 2 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 2 of 3
Mat & Quiet: Compose visitor persona 3 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 3 of 3

Mat & Quiet: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D1, never just shrink..

Mat & Quiet: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D2, never just shrink..

Mat & Quiet: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. D3 gets its own arrangement from the book — the yoga atelier reads differently here..

Mat & Quiet: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D4, never just shrink..

Mat & Quiet: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. D5 gets its own arrangement from the book — the yoga atelier reads differently here..

Mat & Quiet: Reason about colour — what works where — Global colour law locked: hero washes, card tints and CTA styles are chosen per page from RECIPE_POOL — every recipe must clear its WCAG target before it is allowed. The palette (Fern Vista, triadic) provides the roles; dark-mode tokens re-derive and re-check.

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a yoga atelier sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a yoga atelier

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a yoga atelier site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the yoga atelier spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the yoga atelier's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.

Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.

log.entry: Commission accepted: The Wilder Clay — ceramics workshop in PortEllen

The Wilder Clay: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a ceramics workshop the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
The Wilder Clay: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).
The Wilder Clay: Compose visitor persona 1 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 1 of 3
The Wilder Clay: Compose visitor persona 2 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 2 of 3
The Wilder Clay: Compose visitor persona 3 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 3 of 3
The Wilder Clay: Map the journey of persona 1 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — journey 1 of 3
The Wilder Clay: Map the journey of persona 2 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — journey 2 of 3
The Wilder Clay: Map the journey of persona 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — journey 3 of 3

The Wilder Clay: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. D1 gets its own arrangement from the book — the ceramics workshop reads differently here..

The Wilder Clay: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. D2 gets its own arrangement from the book — the ceramics workshop reads differently here..

The Wilder Clay: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. D3 gets its own arrangement from the book — the ceramics workshop reads differently here..

The Wilder Clay: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. D4 gets its own arrangement from the book — the ceramics workshop reads differently here..

The Wilder Clay: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D5, never just shrink..

The Wilder Clay: Reason about colour — what works where — Global colour law locked: hero washes, card tints and CTA styles are chosen per page from RECIPE_POOL — every recipe must clear its WCAG target before it is allowed. The palette (Rosewood Rally, analogous) provides the roles; dark-mode tokens re-derive and re-check.
The Wilder Clay: Lock the brief — audience, tone, promise — deterministic solver — brief composed from niche grammar, consistent with the reasoner’s findings
The Wilder Clay: Lock the palette — harmony math + WCAG — deterministic solver — harmony math + WCAG battery already passed
The Wilder Clay: Choose the D1 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 20 D1 layouts
The Wilder Clay: Choose the D2 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 23 D2 layouts

The Wilder Clay: Reason about the catalog — what the products must do — Catalog law for 0 products: every product needs a name a regular would actually say, a one-line description with a concrete fact, and a price with no hidden extras. Each product earns its own detail page, its own image slot, its own alt text.
The Wilder Clay: Plan the page map — every page earns its slot — deterministic solver — 16 pages planned (content + functional, multi-page mandate)

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a ceramics workshop sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a ceramics workshop

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a ceramics workshop site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the ceramics workshop spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the ceramics workshop's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a ceramics workshop visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

brief.audience: ceramics workshop regulars who notice details
brief.promise: Mud, made honest. The Wilder Clay keeps that promise in PortEllen.
brief.cityStory: We fire in small kiln loads and glaze in-house from tested recipes — and we do it in PortEllen.

D1.why: Poster Stack — Eyebrow → H1 → lede → stacked full-width CTAs → visual below; every block spans the 608px content width. (source: NN/g mobile UX: single-column scanning; iOS HIG poster hierarchy)

D2.why: Ledger Two — The rail survives as a 200px column beside a 2-col body; headline spans both. (source: F-pattern with rail at tablet width)

D3.why: Card Solo — One rounded card floats on the ambient motif holding headline+CTA; content sections plain. (source: Elevated hero card on ambient field (Material elevation))

D4.why: Folio — Story becomes a magazine spread: 7/5 asymmetric columns, drop cap, accent pull-quote spanning the narrow field. (source: Müller-Brockmann asymmetric fields; MDN magazine grid (spans across rows))

D5.why: Ultra Monolith — Edge-to-edge dark field; poster type; 1560px body container. (source: v2 Monolith at ultra)

rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.

The city and the niche vocabulary must appear naturally.
Every internal link must resolve to a generated file.
D1–D5 media blocks present; the page’s per-device layout overrides stamped.
Nav identical to every other page (consistency law).
Review law [popup-walls]: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
Review law [autoplay-sound]: Media stays silent until clicked.
Review law [carousel-ignore]: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
Review law [speed-death]: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
Review law [forced-accounts]: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
Review law [contact-hunt]: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
Review law [about-trust]: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
Review law [tiny-type]: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
Review law [pdf-hate]: Information as real web pages.
Review law [dead-links]: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
Review law [dark-patterns]: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
Review law [cookie-fatigue]: No banner because no tracking.
Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.
Review law [mobile-broken]: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.
Review law [nav-drift]: The same nav, same spot, every page.
Review law [a11y-neglect]: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
Review law [form-fatigue]: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
Review law [og-lies]: A real preview image and honest title/description.
Review law [legal-wall]: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
Review law [stale-copyright]: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
Review law [review-farming]: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
Review law [hidden-prices]: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
Review law [shipping-surprise]: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
knowledge: Robin Williams, The Non-Designer’s Design Book (1994) — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, Proximity

Concrete nouns beat adjectives; a numeral or proper noun must appear where possible.
Banned words: best, world-class, amazing, unbeatable, #1.
The city and the niche vocabulary must appear naturally.
Every internal link must resolve to a generated file.
D1–D5 media blocks present; the page’s per-device layout overrides stamped.
Nav identical to every other page (consistency law).
Review law [popup-walls]: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
Review law [autoplay-sound]: Media stays silent until clicked.
Review law [carousel-ignore]: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
Review law [speed-death]: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
Review law [forced-accounts]: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
Review law [contact-hunt]: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
Review law [about-trust]: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
Review law [tiny-type]: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
Review law [pdf-hate]: Information as real web pages.
Review law [dead-links]: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
Review law [dark-patterns]: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
Review law [cookie-fatigue]: No banner because no tracking.
Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.
Review law [mobile-broken]: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.
Review law [nav-drift]: The same nav, same spot, every page.
Review law [a11y-neglect]: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
Review law [form-fatigue]: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
Review law [og-lies]: A real preview image and honest title/description.
Review law [legal-wall]: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
Review law [stale-copyright]: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
Review law [review-farming]: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
Review law [hidden-prices]: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
Review law [shipping-surprise]: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
knowledge: Robin Williams, The Non-Designer’s Design Book (1994) — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, Proximity
MDN — prefers-color-scheme & relative units

Every internal link must resolve to a generated file.
D1–D5 media blocks present; the page’s per-device layout overrides stamped.
Nav identical to every other page (consistency law).
Review law [popup-walls]: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
Review law [autoplay-sound]: Media stays silent until clicked.
Review law [carousel-ignore]: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
Review law [speed-death]: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
Review law [forced-accounts]: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
Review law [contact-hunt]: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
Review law [about-trust]: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
Review law [tiny-type]: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
Review law [pdf-hate]: Information as real web pages.
Review law [dead-links]: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
Review law [dark-patterns]: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
Review law [cookie-fatigue]: No banner because no tracking.
Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.
Review law [mobile-broken]: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.
Review law [nav-drift]: The same nav, same spot, every page.
Review law [a11y-neglect]: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
Review law [form-fatigue]: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
Review law [og-lies]: A real preview image and honest title/description.
Review law [legal-wall]: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
Review law [stale-copyright]: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
Review law [review-farming]: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
Review law [hidden-prices]: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
Review law [shipping-surprise]: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
